highlights.text: a single-meaning root: "strength" and "intensity."
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: the root's single sense

highlights.text: al-azr: simply "strength" or "power."
I braced my azr [my strength/support] for him with a resolute man's firm resolve
highlights.note: al-Baʿīth, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: a seething, hissing sound
highlights.note: al-Zamakhsharī's literal sense of the root

highlights.text: to incite or goad someone into something, driving him to it through agitation or harassment (izʿāj).
core sense is a kind of livestock — specifically sheep.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: الضَّأْن (al-ḍaʾn) = sheep (as a flock/kind of livestock).
one core idea: uncovering and coming into view.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: الضَّحِك (ḍaḥik) — laughter, the laughing of a human being
الضَّحْو (al-ḍaḥw) is the day's rising; الضُّحى (al-ḍuḥā) is slightly later
"you shall not thirst therein, nor taḍḥā" and glosses it: the sun's heat does not harm you.
highlights.note: تَضْحَىٰ, 1x: the entry's own gloss of Q 20:119

highlights.text: الأُضْحِية (al-uḍḥiya) is the animal offered in sacrifice
Two sound roots gathered under this spelling
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: two separate origins under one spelling

highlights.text: the more analogically sound one takes ḍabḥan as the sound of the racing horses' breath
two words that do not share a common derivational basis (qiyās).
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: the two words share no derivational basis

highlights.text: The ḍidd of a thing is its opposite.
ḍ-f-d-ʿ — "frog."
highlights.note: the root's sense in Lisān al-ʿArab

highlights.text: Normally ضَفادِع (ḍafādiʿ, "frogs")
A verse by the poet Labīd ibn Rabīʿah describes travelers heading to springs at Lubnā or Ajā that are muḍafdiʿāt ("frog-filled")
highlights.note: Labīd ibn Rabīʿah, lived into Islam

highlights.text: covering/concealing something together with a leaning or crookedness
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core meaning for the root

highlights.text: al-ḍighn/al-ḍaghan — the chief derived sense, meaning concealed ill-will or grudge
A verse of Ibn Muqbil uses the same verb for tucking a weapon at one's flank-strap.
things being mixed up and tangled together
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single idea for the root

highlights.text: aḍghāth are dreams that are confused and run together.
A ḍighth is a handful of twigs or of grass
highlights.note: ضِغْث, a bundle taken in the hand

highlights.text: resemblance, matching one thing to another.
highlights.note: the root's core sense in Lisān al-ʿArab

highlights.text: Al-muḍāhāh = to resemble or match something
(they resemble the saying of earlier disbelievers)
Abū Isḥāq explains it as: they resembled the earlier disbelievers' saying, i.e. they said it only in imitation of them
highlights.note: exegete Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj (d. 923) on Q 9:30

highlights.text: A ḥadīth: "the people most severely punished on Judgment Day are those who yuḍāhūn God's creation"
highlights.note: a hadith, taken to cover image-makers

highlights.text: lying flat against the ground on one's side
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: ḍajaʿa, verbal noun ḍujūʿ — to lie down on one's side
highlights.note: مَضَاجِع, 3x "the beds" — places of lying down

highlights.text: a thing being lost and going off where it ought not to go.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single meaning for the root

highlights.text: al-ḍalāl and al-ḍalāla mean the same thing.
Anyone who swerves from the right, intended course is ḍāll, "astray."
a fitting-together (mulāʾama) of two things.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: ḍamamtu l-shayʾa ilā l-shayʾ means "I joined one thing to another"
the root d-m-r has two distinct, sound senses
damara (verb), dumur (verbal noun): said of a horse (or anything else) growing lean, from lightness of flesh
two distinct, valid roots (with few derived words)
aḍ-ḍank (الضَّنْكُ) — narrowness, constriction.
that indicates stinginess with a thing.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: ḍanintu bi-l-shayʾ, aḍannu bihi: "I was grudging of the thing, I am grudging of it"
A rajul ḍanīn is a stingy man.
softness or pliancy in a thing
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: ḍaraʿa al-rajul, verbal noun ḍarāʿa — for a man to become abased or humble himself.
named for its weakness, since it "neither fattens nor avails against hunger."
a line of Ibn Waʿla contrasting patience with slackness
highlights.note: Ibn Waʿla, era undated in the entry

highlights.text: a saying of the Prophet about Jaʿfar's two sons: "Why is it that I see the two of them ḍāriʿayn?"
one root meaning — "to strike a blow"
ضَرَبَ = to strike, inflict a blow on another
الضَّرْب فِي الأَرْض = striking out into the land — journeying, for trade or otherwise
Qur'an 4:101, "when you journey through the land, no blame to shorten the prayer."
highlights.note: the entry's own citation of Q 4:101

highlights.text: three root meanings (uṣūl): the opposite of benefit, the gathering together of a thing, and strength.
Al-ḍarr is the opposite of benefit (nafʿ): ḍarrahu yaḍurruhu ḍarran, "he harmed him."
Iḍṭarra, "to be driven to something," comes from ḍarūra, necessity.
Al-ḍarīr is also someone harmed by the loss of his sight or by the wasting of his body.
Poets also use the form ḍārūra, as Ibn al-Dumayna does
highlights.note: Ibn al-Dumayna, Umayyad (no earlier poet named)

highlights.text: whose one meaning is light.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's one meaning for the root

highlights.text: equivalent to ضِيَاء (ḍiyāʾ, radiance) and نُور (nūr, light).
He cites 2:17, "and when it lit up what was around him" (fa-lammā aḍāʾat mā ḥawlahu)
highlights.note: أَضَاءَ, 3x — the entry's citation of Q 2:17

highlights.text: the loss, disappearance, and perishing of a thing.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: The causative أَضَاعَ / أَضَعْتُ (aḍāʿa / aḍaʿtu) = "to cause something to be lost, to let it go to waste."
one thing inclining or leaning toward another
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's one meaning for the root

highlights.text: ضِفْتُ الرَّجُلَ = I presented myself to a man so he would take me in; أَضَفْتُهُ and ضَيَّفْتُهُ = I lodged him with me
ضَيْف serves for both singular and plural, and also takes the plurals أَضْيَاف and ضِيفَان.
Imruʾ al-Qays: "when we entered it, we propped our backs against every new striped Ḥīran cushion"
he cites a ḥadīth forbidding the ṣalāh when the sun has so inclined toward setting
highlights.note: a hadith on the time of ṣalāh

highlights.text: ضِيق (ḍīq) is the opposite of "roominess" — narrowness, straitness.
highlights.note: the root's core sense in Lisān al-ʿArab

highlights.text: ضاقَ ("became narrow"), with verbal nouns ḍīq and ḍayq
ḍayq is the narrow thing itself; ḍīq is the abstract verbal noun.
Qurʾan 11:12, "...and your breast being straitened (ḍāʾiq) by it."
al-Aʿshā: God "lifted the ḍayqa [hardship] from us"
ḍāqa is given as the plural of ḍāʾiq (Zuhayr's line "narrow of resting-ground")
one underlying sense, which he equates with al-ḍayr and al-maḍarra — "harm."
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: The verb yaḍīru is given as equivalent to yaḍurru ("to harm")
